title: Week 1 review and mini mock test
goal: Use Days 1-6 together in new situations: a real incident, a bug hunt, a one-liner to script, and one small script that combines everything.
setup: # P1: an incident: the to-do backend does not start
printf '#!/bin/bash\necho "todo-backend v2 started" >> logs/app.log && echo "started OK"\n' > incident/releases/v2/start.sh
# P3: log folder with a space in the name, and a broken rotate script

printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/bash' '# Usage: rotate-logs.sh <log-folder>' '# Move every .log file into <log-folder>/old/ and write a summary to rotate.log' 'DIR=$1' 'if [ -z "$DIR" ]; then echo "usage: rotate-logs.sh <log-folder>"; exit 0; fi' 'mkdir $DIR/old' 'for f in $DIR/*.log; do' '  mv $f $DIR/old/' 'done' 'echo "moved $(ls "$DIR/old" | wc -l) files" > rotate.log' > rotate-logs.sh
printf '%s\n' 'server {' '    listen 443 ssl;' '    server_name todo.example.com;' '}' > nginx-tls.conf
# P5: one good and one bad release folder
for r in rel-good rel-bad; do

printf '%s\n' '10.0.0.1 GET /api/todos 200' '10.0.0.2 GET /api/todos 500' '10.0.0.1 POST /api/todos 201' '10.0.0.3 GET /health 200' '10.0.0.2 GET /api/todos 500' '10.0.0.1 GET /api/todos 200' > access.log

warmup.q: Why does `[ $BRANCH = main ]` fail when BRANCH is empty?
warmup.a: The empty variable disappears, so `[` gets `= main`: `unary operator expected`. Quote it or use `[[ ]]`.
Sends stdout to the file, then stderr to the same place. Both end up in the file.

warmup.q: What does `chmod 640` give to owner, group and others?
How do you replace an existing symlink `current` in one command?

problems.title: Incident: the backend does not start
problems.situation: Monday morning. The to-do backend does not start after the weekend deploy. Running `./current/start.sh` says `No such file or directory`. The security team also says the password file is too open. Find and fix three problems.
task: In `incident`, run `./current/start.sh`. Read the error. Check the link with `ls -l current` and `ls releases`.
Point `current` to the release that exists. Run the start script again.
The script now fails to write its log. Check `ls -ld logs` and fix the folder so the owner can write.
Run the start script again until it prints `started OK`. Show `logs/app.log`.
Fix the permission of `.env` so only the owner can read it. Show it with `stat`.
hints: `ln -sfn releases/v2 current` replaces the link. `logs` is 555: no `w` for anyone.
solution: readlink current                  # points to releases/v3, which does not exist
ln -sfn releases/v2 current       # problem 1: broken symlink
chmod 755 logs                    # problem 2: folder not writable
chmod 600 .env                    # problem 3: secret readable by others

explanation.meaning: The symlink `current` points to `releases/v3`, which does not exist (a broken link).
Replace the link in one step (Day 1).
The folder `logs` is 555. To create a file inside a folder, the user needs `w` on the folder (Day 3).
The script appends to the log, then prints OK only if that worked (Day 4).
Secrets: only the owner can read and write.

problems.expected_output:
bash: ./current/start.sh: No such file or directory
exit code: 127
v2
releases/v3
./current/start.sh: line 2: logs/app.log: Permission denied
exit code: 1
555 logs
started OK
todo-backend v2 started
600 .env
mistakes: Running `ln -s releases/v2 current` without `-fn`: the old link is not replaced (`ln: failed to create symbolic link 'current': File exists`).
Fixing with `chmod 777 logs`. It works, but every user can now delete the logs. Use 755.
Stopping after the first fix. In incidents there is often more than one problem. Run the command again after each fix.

checks.expect: ln: failed to create symbolic link 'current': File exists

problems.interview_say: I read the error, fix one thing, and run again. Here the `current` symlink was broken, the logs folder was not writable, and the `.env` file was too open.
problems.try_yourself: Write the three checks as one script that prints OK or FAIL for each (Day 6 file tests: `-e current`, `-w logs`, and the `stat` number for `.env`).

problems.title: Predict the output: a mixed quiz
problems.situation: This is like a written interview test. Each line mixes quotes, variables, redirects and exit codes. The user writes the answers on paper first, then runs the lines one by one.
task: `echo hello > a.txt; echo world > a.txt; cat a.txt`
`ls /nope 2> /dev/null; echo "exit=$?"`
`X=1; ( X=2; echo "in=$X" ); echo "out=$X"`
`[ -d /tmp ] && echo dir || echo nodir` and `[[ abc == a* ]] && echo match`
hints: Single quotes stop replacement. `$(( ))` does math.
`>` overwrites. `2>` sends only errors. `ls` gives exit code 2 for a missing file.
A subshell `( )` has its own copy of variables. Braces make all combinations.
solution: echo hello > a.txt; echo world > a.txt; cat a.txt

explanation.meaning: 5, then the literal text $N, then 10.
The second `>` replaces the first line: only `world` stays.
The error is hidden, but the exit code is still 2.
The subshell change does not come back.
Brace expansion makes every combination: a-1 a-2 b-1 b-2.

problems.expected_output:
5 $N 10
world
exit=2
in=2
out=1
dir
match
a-1 a-2 b-1 b-2
mistakes: Thinking `2> /dev/null` changes the exit code. It only hides the message.
Expecting `out=2`. Changes inside `( )` are lost when the subshell ends.
problems.interview_say: I can predict this because I know the rules: single quotes are literal, `>` overwrites, `2>` only moves errors, and a subshell has its own copy of variables.
problems.try_yourself: Write 3 new quiz lines for a friend, using `>>`, `tee` and `case`. Run them to check your own answers.

problems.title: Find the bug: the log rotate script
problems.situation: `rotate-logs.sh` moves all `.log` files of a folder into `old/`. It works on the test server, but fails on the real one, where the folder is called `app logs`. It also returns 0 when the user forgets the argument, so Jenkins shows green.
task: Run `bash rotate-logs.sh "app logs"`. Read the errors.
Run `bash rotate-logs.sh; echo $?` with no argument. Is the exit code correct?
Find 4 bugs: the usage exit code and stream, `mkdir`, and two quoting problems.
Fix them. Run the fixed script **twice** on `"app logs"` (the second run must not fail). Check with `ls -R "app logs"` and `cat rotate.log`.
hints: Usage errors: message to stderr (`>&2`) and `exit 2`.
`mkdir` without `-p` fails when `old` already exists (second run).
Quote `"$DIR"/old` and `"$f"`. Keep the `*.log` outside the quotes so the wildcard still works: `"$DIR"/*.log`.
solution: rmdir app                          # the broken run made a stray folder "app"
# Move every .log file into <log-folder>/old/ and write a summary to rotate.log
if [ -z "$DIR" ]; then echo "usage: rotate-logs.sh <log-folder>" >&2; exit 2; fi
[ -e "$f" ] || continue          # no .log files: the pattern stays as text
bash rotate-logs.sh "app logs" && bash rotate-logs.sh "app logs"; echo "exit code: $?"

explanation.meaning: Bug 1: usage went to stdout with exit 0. Now it goes to stderr and returns 2 (wrong usage).
Bug 2+3: without quotes, `mkdir $DIR/old` became `mkdir app logs/old`. It made a stray folder `app` and failed on `logs/old`. Without `-p` it also fails on the second run.
Quote the variable part only. The `*` must be outside quotes to match files.
Bug 4: `worker 2.log` has a space; without quotes `mv` got two names.
If no file matches, the loop gets the text `app logs/*.log`. Skip it.

problems.expected_output:
mkdir: cannot create directory ‘logs/old’: No such file or directory
mv: target 'logs/old/': No such file or directory
mv: target 'logs/old/': No such file or directory
ls: cannot access 'app logs/old': No such file or directory
usage: rotate-logs.sh <log-folder>
exit code: 0
usage: rotate-logs.sh <log-folder>
exit code: 2
exit code: 0
'app logs':
old

'app logs/old':
 api.log   web.log  'worker 2.log'
moved 3 files
mistakes: Quoting the wildcard too: `"$DIR/*.log"` looks for a file really named `*.log`.
Testing only once. Many scripts break on the second run (not idempotent). Day 22 covers this.
problems.interview_say: I quote every variable, use `mkdir -p` so a script can run twice, and send usage errors to stderr with a non-zero exit code so CI fails correctly.
problems.try_yourself: Run `shellcheck rotate-logs.sh` on the old version (copy it from the setup line). How many warnings does it show?

problems.title: Convert a one-liner into a safe script
problems.situation: A teammate checks TLS with this one-liner: `grep -q "listen 443" nginx.conf && echo "TLS on" || echo "TLS off"`. The team wants a script for CI: it takes the file as an argument, checks the file exists, and returns exit code 0 (TLS on), 1 (TLS off) or 2 (bad usage).
task: Create `check-tls.sh`. If no argument is given, print usage to stderr and exit 2.
If the file does not exist (`-f`), print an error to stderr and exit 2.
Use `grep -q` in an `if`. Print `TLS on: <file>` and exit 0, or `TLS off: <file>` and exit 1.
Test with `nginx-tls.conf`, `nginx-plain.conf`, `missing.conf`, and no argument. Print the exit code after each run.
hints: Use a regex that allows more spaces: `grep -Eq 'listen[[:space:]]+443' "$CONF"`.
Loop for the test: `for f in nginx-tls.conf nginx-plain.conf missing.conf ""; do bash check-tls.sh $f; echo "exit: $?"; done`.
solution: # Usage: check-tls.sh <nginx.conf>   exit 0 = TLS on, 1 = TLS off, 2 = usage error
for f in nginx-tls.conf nginx-plain.conf missing.conf ""; do

explanation.meaning: Guard: stop early with usage when the argument is missing.
Check the file exists before reading it.
`-E` extended regex, `-q` quiet (only the exit code).
One or more spaces or tabs. More robust than one exact space.
Different codes so CI can tell "off" from "broken input".

problems.expected_output:
TLS on: nginx-tls.conf
exit: 0
TLS off: nginx-plain.conf
exit: 1
error: missing.conf not found
exit: 2
usage: check-tls.sh <nginx.conf>
exit: 2
mistakes: Keeping `A && B || C` in the script: if `B` fails, `C` also runs. An `if` block is clearer.
Printing errors to stdout. Other tools that read stdout get confused. Errors go to `>&2`.
problems.interview_say: When I turn a one-liner into a script, I add argument checks, file checks, clear messages on stderr, and meaningful exit codes, so it works well in CI.
problems.try_yourself: Make the script accept many files: loop over `"$@"` and exit 1 if any file has TLS off.

problems.title: Mini project: release-check.sh
problems.situation: Before a release goes live, a script must check the release folder and write a short report file for the team chat. This combines Week 1: arguments, file tests, permissions, variables, a here-doc, redirects and exit codes.
task: Write `release-check.sh <folder>`. Check the argument and that the folder exists (`-d`).
Check: `VERSION` is not empty (`-s`), `start.sh` is executable (`-x`), `.env` has permission 600 (`stat -c %a`).
Count problems. Write `report.txt` with a here-doc: folder, version, number of problems, and the result PASS or FAIL.
Print the report. Exit 0 if no problems, else exit 1.
Run it on `rel-good` and `rel-bad` and print the exit code each time.
hints: Keep a variable `PROBLEMS=0` and a list `NOTES=""`. Add to both when a check fails.
Version: `VERSION=$(cat "$DIR/VERSION" 2>/dev/null)` and use `${VERSION:-unknown}` in the report.
solution: [ -d "$DIR" ] || { echo "error: $DIR is not a folder" >&2; exit 2; }
if [ "$PROBLEMS" -eq 0 ]; then RESULT=PASS; else RESULT=FAIL; fi

explanation.meaning: Wrong usage stops the script before any check.
A tiny function: count the problem and remember the message (functions are Day 9).
A real new line character, so each note is on its own line.
Here-doc with variables (unquoted delimiter), Day 4.
Default text when the version is empty.
The last command decides the exit code of the script: 0 for PASS, 1 for FAIL.

problems.expected_output:
Release check: rel-good
Version:  3.0.0
Problems: 0
Result:   PASS
exit code: 0

Release check: rel-bad
Version:  unknown
Problems: 3
- VERSION is missing or empty
- start.sh is not executable
- .env permission is 664, must be 600
Result:   FAIL
exit code: 1
mistakes: Indenting the here-doc lines in the real file: the spaces go into the report. Keep report lines at the start of the line (or use `<<-` with tabs).
Calling `stat` on a missing `.env`: `stat: cannot statx 'rel-x/.env': No such file or directory` (Ubuntu 22.04 says `cannot stat`). Check `-e` first in a real script.

checks.expect: stat: cannot statx 'rel-x/.env': No such file or directory

problems.interview_say: My release check validates input, runs each check, collects problems, writes a report with a here-doc, and returns 0 or 1 so the pipeline can stop a bad release.
problems.try_yourself: Add a fourth check: the folder must have a `README.md`. Then add `--quiet` as a second argument that hides the report but keeps the exit code.

problems.title: Status code summary from an access log
problems.situation: The team lead asks for a quick summary in the chat: how many requests had each status code, and which IP made the most 500 errors. The log is `access.log` (IP, method, URL, status).
task: Print the count of each status code with `awk '{print $4}'`, `sort` and `uniq -c`.
Save that summary to `status.txt` and show it on the screen at the same time (`tee`).
Find the IPs with 500 errors and count them per IP.
hints: `awk '{print $4}' access.log` prints the 4th word of each line (awk is Day 11, here only this one form).
solution: awk '{print $4}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | tee status.txt

explanation.meaning: Print field 4 (the status code). Fields are split by spaces.
Group equal lines and count them (Day 2).
Show and save at the same time (Day 4).
Only lines that end with ` 500`.

mistakes: Using double quotes around the awk code: `awk "{print $4}"`. Bash replaces `$4` (empty) first, so awk prints whole lines.
`grep 500` without anchors also matches `/api/500-items` or a size of 1500 bytes.
problems.interview_say: To summarise a log I cut the field I need, then `sort | uniq -c`. I anchor grep patterns to avoid false matches.
problems.try_yourself: Add `| sort -rn | head -n 1` to get only the most common status code.

interview.a: Absolute starts at `/` and works from anywhere. Relative starts from the current folder.
Hard link = second name for the same data (survives delete). Symlink = path to a target (breaks if the target is deleted, can point to folders).

interview.q: Rapid 3: How do you show the last 50 lines of a log and keep watching?
Rapid 5: Does root obey file permissions?
interview.a: Mostly no. Root ignores read and write permissions. 'Others' means other normal users, not root.

interview.q: Rapid 7: How do you hide all output of a command?

interview.a: Single: literal, nothing replaced. Double: variables and `$( )` replaced, spaces kept together.
It makes a variable visible to child processes (scripts and programs started from this shell).

interview.q: Rapid 10: What exit code means success, and how do you see it?
interview.a: 0 means success. `echo $?` right after the command shows it.

recap.meaning: Show where a symlink points (find broken links)
Permissions of the folder itself, not its content
Permission as a number (for script checks)
Quote the variable, keep the wildcard outside
Usage error to stderr with exit code 2

coverage.item: One small script that combines everything
